# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: From Initial Promise to Future Perspectives

## Introduction
Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has evolved significantly since its inception, progressing from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents and drug-eluting metallic stents (DES). Although contemporary DES have dramatically reduced restenosis and stent thrombosis, they permanently cage the vessel, preventing physiological vasomotion, inducing chronic vessel-wall inflammation, and impeding potential future coronary artery bypass grafting. The concept of "vascular reparative therapy" emerged to overcome these limitations, utilizing temporary bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) that provide mechanical support and drug elution during the critical healing phase before dissolving into inert end-products.

## Early Development and the Absorb Era
The history of bioresorbable devices began with the non-drug-eluting Igaki-Tamai polymeric scaffold [1]. This was followed by the development of the Absorb everolimus-eluting BVS (Abbott Vascular), constructed from a poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) backbone with a strut thickness of approximately 150 µm. Initial first-in-human and cohort studies demonstrated feasible mechanical support, progressive scaffold resorption within three to four years, and restoration of vasomotor function [2,3].

These early-phase findings paved the way for large-scale, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing the Absorb BVS against the gold-standard metallic everolimus-eluting stent (EES; Xience). The 1-year results of the ABSORB II [4], ABSORB III [5], ABSORB China [6], and ABSORB Japan [7] trials demonstrated non-inferior clinical outcomes regarding target lesion failure (TLF).

## The Safety Signal and Market Withdrawal
As longer-term follow-up data accumulated, a significant safety signal emerged. The 3-year outcomes of the ABSORB II trial [8], along with the 2-year [9] and 3-year [10] results of ABSORB III, revealed a higher incidence of TLF and scaffold thrombosis (ScT) with Absorb BVS compared with metallic EES. The Amsterdam Investigator-Initiated Absorb Registry (AIDA) trial was prematurely halted due to safety concerns regarding a nearly four-fold increase in ScT [11].

Large-scale patient-level meta-analyses confirmed these findings, indicating that Absorb BVS was associated with an increased risk of both early and late ScT, as well as target-vessel myocardial infarction [12,13]. Long-term data, including the 3-year outcomes of ABSORB China [14] and the final 5-year outcomes of ABSORB III [15], established that the hazard of ScT remained elevated until full resorption occurred at 3–4 years. Consequently, the device was withdrawn from the commercial market, and clinical guidelines downgraded its use to a Class III (harmful) recommendation [16].

## Mechanistic Insights and Implantation Techniques
Intracoronary imaging, particularly optical coherence tomography (OCT), provided vital insights into the mechanisms of BVS failure [17]. The thick struts (150 µm) of the first-generation Absorb BVS disrupted laminar blood flow, causing local rheological disturbances, delayed endothelialization, and a propensity for platelet aggregation [18]. Furthermore, late scaffold disassembly prior to complete resorption, strut malapposition, and accelerated neoatherosclerosis were identified as primary drivers of very late ScT [19].

In response, investigators highlighted the critical role of procedural optimization. The "PSP" protocol—comprising meticulous vessel **P**reparation, accurate **S**izing (avoiding small vessels <2.25 mm), and high-pressure **P**ost-dilation—was shown to significantly reduce the risk of ScT and adverse events [20]. This strategy was prospectively validated in the ABSORB IV trial, which demonstrated improved clinical safety when BVS was implanted using optimized technique in appropriately sized vessels [21]. Real-world registries, such as GHOST-EU, corroborated the importance of procedural technique in optimizing patient selection and outcomes [22].

## Next-Generation Scaffolds and Future Directions
The clinical setbacks of first-generation PLLA devices underscored the need for thinner struts and alternative materials. Current research focuses on two main paths: magnesium-based metallic scaffolds and thin-strut polymeric scaffolds [23].

Magnesium-based scaffolds, such as the Magmaris (Biotronik), offer greater radial strength, allowing for a faster resorption process (approximately 12 months) and a better safety profile [24]. The BIOSOLVE-II trial demonstrated excellent safety and vascular healing at 6 months [25], which was sustained through 3 years of follow-up [26]. The BIOSOLVE-IV registry further confirmed the safety of this magnesium-based BVS in a larger, real-world population, showing low rates of target lesion failure and scaffold thrombosis [27].

Concurrently, advances in polymer technology have yielded ultra-thin strut devices. The FANTOM II trial evaluated the Fantom scaffold (REVA Medical), a sirolimus-eluting tyrosine polycarbonate-based scaffold with 125 µm struts, showing favorable clinical and angiographic outcomes [28]. Even thinner PLLA-based devices have emerged, such as the MeRes100 (100 µm struts) [29] and the Firesorb (86 µm struts) [30], both demonstrating promising safety and efficacy profiles in early clinical trials.

## Conclusion
The journey of BVS in PCI represents a classic paradigm of translational medicine. While the first-generation Absorb BVS failed due to mechanical limitations and thick struts, it established the feasibility of complete vascular restoration. Through procedural optimization (PSP) and the development of next-generation thin-strut polymeric and bioresorbable metallic technologies, the field of interventional cardiology continues to strive toward the goal of "leaving nothing behind."
